endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: It is important to clarify whether the implementer team’s organization monitors and sunsets AI algorithms that are no longer supported and assess whether there is a plan for handling developer-driven EOL processes.

endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Who manages decommissioning or modifications if performance degrades?

endorsements.title: Health Equity Across the AI Lifecycle (HEAAL) framework
endorsements.issuer: Health AI Partnership; PLOS Digital Health (PMID 38723025, doi:10.1371/journal.pdig.0000390)
endorsements.quote: If the monitoring results diverge from these objectives, the AI solution undergoes either updates or decommissioning.

endorsements.title: Developing, purchasing, implementing and monitoring AI tools in radiology: practical considerations. A multi-society statement
endorsements.issuer: ACR, CAR, ESR, RANZCR, RSNA; Radiol Artif Intell 2024 (PMID 38251899, doi:10.1148/ryai.230513)
endorsements.quote: and an orderly process to replace currently deployed products with future updates or alternative products.

endorsements.title: Key decision points in adopting an AI solution
endorsements.issuer: Health AI Partnership (Duke Health and partners)
endorsements.quote: Also includes guides for minimizing disruptions and harms that result from decommissioning AI products and disseminating information about AI product updates to affected clinicians.

commentary.bottom_line: Five frameworks and guidance documents endorse assigning responsibility for revising or decommissioning AI tools when monitoring shows degradation, drift, or equity shortfalls, but no supplied study tests whether doing so keeps degraded or inequitable AI out of clinical use. The recommendation rests on expert consensus rather than measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: No study was supplied that tests the practice, and no study was supplied that documents the hazard. The support consists of five endorsements, two using "should" language and three that describe or pose the question. Under GRADE conventions, expert statements do not count as evidence of effect, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

The HEAAL framework states that when monitoring diverges from equity objectives, the tool undergoes updates or decommissioning. This ties the decommissioning decision to equity monitoring, yet no supplied study shows how often equity-triggered retirement occurs or whether it reduces disparities for affected groups.

The endorsing sources are voluntary frameworks and a multi-society radiology statement, and none cites a binding rule. The CHAI guide asks implementers to plan for developer-driven end-of-life processes, which suggests that accountability may be split between vendor and health system unless contracts assign it.

One framework includes guides for limiting disruption when products are retired and for informing affected clinicians of updates, and the radiology statement calls for an orderly replacement process. These sources indicate that decommissioning carries workflow costs, but no supplied study reports staffing, time, or expense for carrying it out.

commentary.research_gap: No study has measured whether naming an accountable owner for revision or decommissioning shortens the time degraded or inequitable AI remains in use, or how often monitoring signals lead to action. Studies comparing organizations with and without assigned ownership, and tracking time from detected drift to remediation, would address this gap.
commentary.underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, so there is no evidence on Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Organizations serving these groups cannot yet know whether equity-triggered decommissioning protects them in practice.
